title: Safety pipeline topology & latency budgeting (KV/batching/quantization tradeoffs)
summary: Redwood SE/AE walked NimbusPay through safety filter placement options and how each impacts tail latency and throughput. Discussed KV/prefix caching, batching windows, and quantization choices; sketched async vs inline moderation tradeoffs and proposed an experimental benchmark plan with traffic-shaped tests on Dedicated and Private (VPC) deployments.
topics: filter placement: inline vs async vs pre-score
KV cache hit patterns and eviction impact
batching window tuning and token budget

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-25 16:00 UTC | Duration: 72m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Derek (Redwood SE), Lina (Redwood SE), Priya (NimbusPay Head of ML), Omar (Nimbus Infra), Samira (PM)

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda - we want to talk topology choices for the safety pipeline and how that impacts latency and throughput for your real-time payflow assistant.
00:14 Priya: Thanks, yeah latency is critical. We have a 200ms soft SLO for 95th, but hard 300ms budget for UI interactivity. Safety can't blow that up.
00:28 Derek: Right. So we typically break the end-to-end token budget into generation time, model pre- and post-processing, and moderation. For inline filters you pay the full RTT. For async you might do speculative returns then rescind, or tag responses with a safety score.
00:46 Omar: Can you clarify speculative returns? Sounds risky for legal/compliance.
00:54 Derek: Yeah, speculative is where you return a fast answer and run a background stronger filter. If it fails, you retract or notify. It adds complexity and audit trails, but can keep 95th latency low. Many enterprise teams prefer deterministic blocking inline for regulatory reasons.
01:13 Priya: We need audit logs + deterministic behavior for PII; speculative retracts are tricky.
01:20 Lina: Noted. Another axis is placement relative to KV cache. If your safety filter runs against raw model tokens, you might not benefit from prefix KV caching; conversely, if you run a filter pre-generation (pre-scoring input) you save model cost but lose context on generated content.
01:36 Samira: So there are three patterns? Pre-filter (on prompt), inline filter (on model output), and post async?
01:45 Derek: Exactly. Pre-filter is cheap but less accurate for hallucinations or emergent failures. Inline is accurate but adds per-request latency. Async gives best perceived latency but complex.
01:58 02:00 Maya: Let's quantify. Suppose baseline generation p95 is 120ms on your Dedicated pool with 1K token/s throughput profile. An inline classifier that runs on the same GPU could add 40-80ms depending on model size and quantization. If classifier is separate service, network hop + batching could add 60-140ms.
02:23 Omar: Wait classifier on GPU — is that another model? Could we do a lightweight CPU check?
02:30 Derek: You could. Many teams run a fast heuristic or small distilled classifier on CPU for quick rejects, then escalate risky items to GPU classifier. The trick is false negatives vs cost.
02:41 Priya: Our taxonomy: PII redaction (hard block), abusive content (soft restrict), policy scoring for downstream analysts. Redaction must be deterministic and logged.
02:52 03:10 Lina: On KV caching — if you have strong prefix cache hit rates, generation latency drops significantly. But batching policies interact: larger batching windows increase throughput but inflate p95. We usually tune batch window to meet latency SLOs while preserving GPU utilization.
03:30 Derek: Practical knob: target micro-batches of 8-16 for low-latency but enable continuous batching when utilization low. Also set a max batching delay (say 10ms) to avoid long tail.
03:44 Priya: Can KV cache evictions cause spikes? We saw a 2-3x p95 spike during cache churn last quarter.
03:52 Derek: Yes. Eviction storms (e.g., new model version or long-tail prompts) cause cache miss storms — that forces full compute and can spike latency. For safety filters, evictions matter because missing KV means classifier may see different context or needs re-run. You can mitigate with warmup loads and sticky routing.
04:10 Samira: Quantization — you mentioned 4-bit for cost. How does that affect safety classifier accuracy?
04:20 Derek: Good question. Lower-bit quant (4-bit/QLoRA-style) reduces memory and can increase throughput, but may degrade nuanced classifier calibration. For redaction/PII we recommend keeping the classifier at higher precision (8-bit) or using ensemble checks — small CPU heuristic + quantized model. You should A/B test with labeled prompts.
04:40 Maya: Also consider mixed-precision: generation quantized for throughput while classifier runs in FP16/8. That keeps safety behavior stable.
04:50 05:05 Omar: For VPC/on-prem constraints — our legal team prefers that moderation traces don't leave our VPC. How does Redwood Private handle that?
05:15 Maya: Private deployment can run the safety pipeline entirely inside your VPC. We integrate with customer KMS and HSM; audit logs remain in your storage. The only thing in control plane is rollout metadata if you opt-in.
05:28 Priya: If we run classifier as a separate private service, can we still use Redwood's KV caching?
05:36 Derek: Yes, but KV placement matters. You can co-locate KV cache with Private runtime (same VPC) to keep traffic internal. Or use an external cache backed by Redis in your network. The key is latency between model and cache — <2ms is ideal to avoid big penalties.
05:52 Lina: One more topology we sometimes recommend: hybrid inline + edge pre-filter. Run a cheap heuristic at the edge to drop obvious cases, run the heavy classifier inline or async depending on policy. That reduces load on main classifier and improves tail.
06:10 Priya: Any data on cost delta inline vs async? We need to justify to finance.
06:18 Derek: Rough rule of thumb — inline classifier co-located on GPU adds GPU-ms cost per request. Async offload to separate service converts cost to extra throughput and storage. For high-volume low-risk traffic, async amortizes cost better. We'll produce a cost-per-1M-requests sketch for your traffic mix.
06:34 Samira: We care about end-to-end consistency. If async labels later and we rescind answers, UX flow must handle it. That's product complexity.
06:42 Maya: Yup, that's why auditability and policy play into topology. For PII redaction, inline deterministic blocks are simplest. For lower-risk policy scoring, async may be fine.
06:54 07:30 Derek: Let's get into specifics for NimbusPay. Priya, what are your prompt length distributions and common token rates?
07:40 Priya: Most prompts are short — 20-60 input tokens; expected generation 10-50 tokens. Peak QPS ~250, 95th concurrent requests translate to ~300 concurrent token streams.
07:56 Derek: With that shape, KV caching of user history/prefix should hit often. For batching, keep micro-batch size small to preserve latency; for off-peak you can increase batch size. Also consider dynamic batching that reduces target batch size as queue latency grows.
08:12 Omar: For cache warm start, can Redwood prewarm keys? We have millions of users - prewarming all keys isn't feasible.
08:21 Derek: You prewarm the hot set and implement an LRU with rate-limited misses. Also use sticky routing for a short window so repeated near-term requests hit same backend.
08:32 Priya: How about safety model architecture? We don't want to maintain lots of models. Is there a single unified model that can do both generation and classification cheaply?
08:41 Lina: Some teams use a single backbone with a classification head. That can save ops but coupling means a generation workload could affect classifier performance and vice versa. Separation gives independent scaling and different quantization choices.
08:55 Derek: Another trick: use shallow early-exit classifier that only examines prefix tokens to quickly filter trivial cases, then escalate to heavier classifier only when needed. That reduces average cost.
09:10 09:30 Priya: Benchmarks — can you run tests that simulate cache hit/miss and realistic batching?
09:35 Derek: Yes. Our benchmark harness can replay your sampled traffic with toggles for cache hit rate, batch window, quantization, and filter placement. We'll send that harness and a config template.
09:45 Maya: We'll also include a latency breakdown template — generation, network, filter, batching delay, and tail percentiles. Fill that in with your targets.
09:56 Samira: Any gotchas with Kubernetes autoscaling and GPU draining that affect latency? We had spikes when nodes drained.
10:03 Derek: Node draining can cause in-flight requests to be rescheduled causing jitter. Use graceful drain with rerouting, and cap scale events during peak windows. Dedicated pools with reserved capacity help avoid surprise drains.
10:17 10:30 Priya: Could you sketch a recommended default for NimbusPay?
10:35 Derek: For your 200ms SLO, conservative proposal:
- Pre-filter at edge (CPU heuristics) for trivial blocks
- Inline lightweight classifier (8-bit FP) co-located with generation for PII redaction (deterministic)
- Async deep classifier for policy scoring (non-blocking) with audit logs
- KV cache co-located in VPC, warm hot keys, sticky routing
- Micro-batch size 8, max batch delay 10ms; scale batch size up during off-peak

10:55 Priya: That sounds reasonable. For redaction we must keep FP16/8 at least, avoid aggressive 4-bit for classifier.
11:05 Derek: Agreed. We'll also recommend thresholding and fallback: if classifier confidence low, escalate to human review or fallback to a conservative redact decision.
11:16 Omar: About fallbacks — is it possible to route to a cheaper small model when the main cluster is saturated?
11:24 Lina: Yes, smart routing can send overflow to a quantized smaller variant or to Dedicated burst capacity. Redwood supports routing policies by latency/cost region and graceful degradation.
11:36 Maya: Final logistics — we'll send the harness, and propose a pilot: run 2 hours of replay with 3 traffic shapes (baseline, 2x QPS, cache-churn) and share results.
11:48 Priya: OK please include the expected metrics table. Also include security posture info for Private deployment.
11:58 Maya: Will do. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with dates.
12:05 Meeting end.

Notes: Transcription contains occasional mis-words (e.g., "quanitization" for quantization in a few spots), speaker overlap near 06:34 resulted in a short garble. Shared artifacts: https://redwood.internal/docs/safety-topologies (deck), benchmark-harness: https://redwood-files/replay/harness.zip
